Lesson 01

Name the job before you name the model

Why it matters

A product sentence has a person, a job, and a constraint. The model is an implementation choice.

Try it: One-page spec

Lesson
01 of 06
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Sentence
Person, job, constraint
Model
After that
Also
A non-goal

Hiring posts for AI product managers in 2026 ask for the same discipline as the engineering tracks: a user, a workflow, a measurement, and a risk. Start with the job-to-be-done.

When a support lead reviews yesterday's refunds,
they need the policy line that applies,
without pasting the whole handbook into a chat,
in under a minute,
with a citation they can forward.

If you cannot fill those clauses, you do not have a feature. You have a model in search of a demo. The citation requirement is what makes this a retrieval product. The minute is a latency budget. The handbook staying put is a privacy requirement. The model choice comes after.

Practice

Write a four-line job statement for something you would actually use. Include a latency or cost constraint and a proof constraint, such as a citation or a test.

Check

Where does the model name belong in the spec?

Show the answer

After the job, the constraint, and the proof. It is a choice you can swap if the eval holds.

Lesson 02

Write a one-page spec

Why it matters

Problem, user, non-goals, success, risks, and the first milestone.

Try it: One-page spec

Lesson
02 of 06
Time
12 min
Level
Practice
Fits
One page
Success
Four numbers
Milestone
The smallest scored release
SectionWhat a builder needs
ProblemThe job statement from 12-01.
UserWho is in the loop, and who is definitely not the user yet.
Non-goalsWhat this version will not do. Unattended send is a good non-goal.
SuccessThe eval gate: quality, safety, latency, cost.
RisksWrong citation, stale policy, injection in a ticket, data leaving the tenant.
MilestoneThe smallest slice that can be scored. Often: ten tasks, one corpus, no tools that write.

One page forces the cut. A ten-page spec that does not name a non-goal will be read as permission to build the platform.

Practice

Fill the six sections in short lines for your job statement. If success has no number or no pass/fail, it is not success yet.

Check

Why write non-goals in the spec?

Show the answer

Because an unnamed non-goal gets built as soon as a demo suggests it.

Lesson 03

Share four numbers with engineering

Why it matters

Quality, safety fails, latency, and cost per successful task.

Try it: Cost and latency

Lesson
03 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Share
One table
Quality
Pass rate
Cost
Per success

A roadmap slide that says 'improve AI quality' does not tell an engineer what to do. The shared numbers do. They are the same four axes as the eval gate, expressed as a product promise.

  • Quality: which tasks, and the pass bar.
  • Safety: which failures are release blockers.
  • Latency: the time the person actually waits, at a percentile you name.
  • Cost: per successful task, including human review time if review is required.

Add a counter-metric so the team cannot game the first number. If you only score deflection, the system will refuse hard tickets and look successful. Pair deflection with a check that the citation was real, or with a sample a person reviews.

Practice

Write the four numbers for your spec, plus one counter-metric. Use targets you could measure this month, not a press-release percentage.

Check

Why is deflection alone a dangerous metric?

Show the answer

The system can push work away, or answer wrongly, and the deflection count still rises.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Latency and quality, as a design sketch

Positions are for a design conversation. They are not a benchmark and they are not a ranking of vendors. A local model is not automatically more accurate. A long window is not automatically more careful.

Lesson 04

Design the empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states

Why it matters

The model will hit all four. The interface should say what happened.

Try it: One-page spec

Lesson
04 of 06
Time
11 min
Level
Practice
Design
Empty, slow, wrong, unsafe
Wrong
Shows the gap
Unsafe
Says what a person can do
StateWhat the person sees
EmptyNo source contained the answer. Offer the search you ran, not a guess.
SlowStill working, with a way to stop. Do not freeze a silent button.
WrongA way to see the citation and mark it bad. That mark becomes an eval task.
UnsafeThe action did not run. Say what was blocked. Do not explain how to get around the block.

A chat box with no states is a demo. A product names these four and logs them. The unsafe state is especially easy to get wrong: a coy message that hints at the blocked action teaches the next try.

Practice

Write the four messages in your product's voice, each in one sentence. Read the unsafe message and delete any hint of a workaround.

Check

What should a 'wrong' answer let the person do?

Show the answer

Open the citation and mark the failure so you can add it to the task set.

Lesson 05

Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release

Why it matters

A limited release has a named audience, a kill switch, and a date you will read the scorecard.

Try it: One-page spec

Lesson
05 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Order
Prototype, eval, limited release
Audience
Named
Off switch
A kill switch
  1. Prototype on synthetic data. Show the empty state on purpose.
  2. Freeze ten tasks and a gate. Do not invite users past a failing gate.
  3. Limited release to people who know it is a draft and know how to report a bad citation.
  4. Read the scorecard on the date you set. Expand, revise, or turn it off.

A kill switch is a flag that disables the model path and leaves the previous workflow intact. If there is no previous workflow, the kill switch is 'stop showing the feature'. Shipping without that flag means an incident becomes a scramble.

Buy versus build

A hosted agent product can be the right milestone if it meets the policy page. You still own the eval and the data question. Buying the UI does not buy the judgment.

Practice

Write the audience for a limited release in one sentence, the kill switch, and the date you will read the numbers.

Check

What has to be true before the limited release?

Show the answer

The gate passes on the frozen tasks, the audience is named, and you can turn the feature off.

Lesson 06

Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed

Why it matters

Speech recognition and speech synthesis are models with their own failure modes. They do not replace the eval.

Try it: Cost and latency

Lesson
06 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Budget
The whole wait
Fallback
Text and a person
Evals
Do not inherit the text score

A voice interface adds two models and a clock. Speech-to-text can drop names, numbers, and domain words. Text-to-speech can say a wrong answer smoothly, which is worse than a wrong paragraph the person can skim. Barge-in, silence, and background noise are product states, not polish.

A minimum voice design

  • A latency budget for the turn, written down. If you cannot meet it, stay on text.
  • A domain word list you tested on, including the names your users actually say.
  • A visible transcript so the person can catch a recognition error.
  • A handoff to a human that the caller can trigger, and that the system triggers when confidence in the retrieved answer is absent.
  • No unattended action. Voice is a draft and a lookup until a person confirms.

If your background is phone systems, bring that operational care to the latency budget and the handoff. Leave the vendor-specific telephony course for a telephony course. Here, voice is an interface on top of the same retrieval, tools, and evals.

Practice

Decide whether your spec needs voice in the first release. If yes, write the latency budget and the handoff sentence. If no, write it as a non-goal.

Check

Why is a smooth spoken answer a higher bar than a written one?

Show the answer

Because the person cannot scan a citation while the sentence is already being said. The transcript and the handoff have to carry the check.
